Later, I sincerely apologized, and she forgave me. Even so, I still feel guilty when I think about it. That experience taught me to be more careful with my words, especially when speaking to the people I love.

In junior high school, I trained for the PE entrance exam by running ten laps around the track every day. I wasn’t good at running, and at first, I was far from meeting the 800-meter target of 3 minutes and 25 seconds. However, after six months of consistent practice, I finished in 3 minutes and 14 seconds in the actual exam. I felt a great sense of achievement and learned that persistence pays off.

One of my most cherished memories from high school was walking home with my close friends after school. Our classes didn’t finish until 10 p.m., and we were under a lot of pressure. Those walks gave us a chance to relax and talk freely about anything on our minds. Sharing our worries and laughter made those stressful days easier and left me with unforgettable memories.

In my final year of high school, my politics grades dropped sharply just before the college entrance exam, and I felt lost. A close friend who excelled in the subject set aside her own study time to help me understand the key concepts and their connections during evening study sessions. With her guidance, my grades gradually improved, and I eventually scored 93 on the exam. Even today, I am deeply moved by her kindness and grateful for her support.

I once had a very close friend. We had so much in common and could talk openly about almost anything. I truly valued our friendship and never imagined that it would end the way it did.

Later, however, I discovered that she had been speaking badly about me to a mutual friend. She had also copied my work for a design assignment. When I confronted her about these things, she firmly denied doing anything wrong. Her reaction hurt me deeply because I had trusted her and hoped we could have an honest conversation about what had happened. After that, I felt I could no longer trust her, so I decided to end our friendship.

Even today, I still miss the happy times we shared. Although I chose to walk away, those good memories still mean a lot to me. Looking back, I feel both hurt by what happened and sad that a friendship I once treasured came to an end.

After leaving home for university, I started learning to cook for myself. One of my most memorable moments was making a bowl of noodles with plenty of meat. I enjoyed a filling meal and felt proud of myself for preparing it on my own.

When I told my mother, she praised me enthusiastically and even said she wanted to reward me. I felt both excited and deeply touched. I hadn’t expected such a small achievement to mean so much to her. Her reaction reminded me that I had grown up with her constant encouragement. This simple experience made me appreciate her love and support even more.

Around the time I graduated from university, a friend and I spent two weeks traveling around northeastern China in winter. We saw beautiful snowy landscapes, admired the ice sculptures in Harbin, and even visited Russia to experience a different culture.

The most unforgettable part of the trip was learning to snowboard. At first, I fell over again and again, but I kept getting back up and trying. After two days of practice, I finally learned the “falling leaf” technique, which allowed me to move down the slope slowly while controlling my speed.

Although snowboarding was tiring and challenging, I found it incredibly fun and rewarding. It absorbed all my attention, and each small improvement gave me a sense of achievement. The experience taught me to be patient with myself and to keep going despite setbacks. That trip sparked my love of snowboarding.

The Best Lunch I've Ever Had — I traveled to Guizhou with my best friend. One day I slept in until noon, and as I was lazing in bed, I felt extremely hungry. Just then, my friend told me she'd already ordered takeout for me — a local noodle soup in broth. It smelled amazing. That turned out to be the most wonderful lunch experience I've ever had! It wasn't anything fancy, but because my best friend had prepared food that hit my taste perfectly at my hungriest moment, it was absolutely wonderful.

About Worship and Faith — In the first half of the year, because I sat for too long without proper rest, my right lower back often hurt. I tried many medicines and physical therapies — tuina massage and acupuncture — but nothing worked. It wasn't until I went to have a meal near Sanyuan Temple in Guangzhou with a friend that we decided to visit the temple on the way. The temple has a fixed fortune-stick drawing ritual, where each participant can prepare a question to ask the gods. I joined in and asked the gods whether my back could recover this year. I drew a fortune stick, and the classical Chinese text on it suggested that I needed to take things slowly and not be impatient for this to be accomplished. I firmly believed in this idea, so I put it into practice for the week after I returned — and my back mysteriously got better. How miraculous!

Frustrating Tutoring Job — I once had a short and bumpy tutoring job as a middle-school teacher, arranged through an agency I found online. At first I thought it would be promising because the pay was quite generous, but what happened later made me furious. When I took the job, I paid the agency a 750 RMB information fee (which they'd promised to refund if the job didn't go through, but keep if it succeeded). I prepared carefully for the trial lesson, and the parent said at first that she was very satisfied with me. But two days after the lesson, she said the student actually wanted a male tutor. I thought, "OK, fine." But the infuriating part was the agency — whenever I contacted them, they kept refusing to refund my fee. After a while, a friend told me I needed to be tougher. So I sent the agency a message on WeChat saying that if they kept making excuses and didn't refund me, I would call the police. They refunded me the very same day. So satisfying!

A Lucky Exam Story — This one is about an exam, and it happened during summer break this year. I was preparing for the IELTS, with less than a month left before my MFA language requirement was due. I was extremely nervous the whole time — right up to the night before the exam, I thought I was doomed and felt underprepared. Even during the exam itself, I misread half the question numbers in the listening section at the very start. But at least I managed to finish everything. After the exam, I was really, really upset, and I didn't even want to talk to my family. They cared about me, but they kept pressing me with questions, which made me feel even worse. Unexpectedly, two days later I received a text message — OMG — I had actually passed the requirement! So I'm very grateful that I stuck with it and completed the test. All I can say is that it was a stroke of luck.

Drifting Apart from Old Friends — My high school friends and I were very close three or four years ago. Even though we were in different cities and countries, we always messaged each other. But starting this year, for some reason, we've been in contact less and less. We never had a fight. Maybe we've just all gotten busier, or maybe our lives have drifted apart, or perhaps some of us started dating. I feel a bit wistful about it, and I hope that someday we can get back to how close we used to be.

Learning Not to Do Too Much at Once — Last week my mom mailed me a huge amount of meat — ribs, pork, beef, shrimp, and so on. I was so happy when it arrived, and I planned to cook for myself every day, at every meal, and I wanted every single meal to be rich and beautiful. But then I realized I couldn't keep up — I was often late for class. Well, this experience taught me that some things are very worth doing, but you shouldn't rush to take on too much all at once.

Getting into Gaming — I used to play very few games, but after starting CMA I noticed that many of my classmates loved gaming, so I downloaded some of the games they talked about. Recently I've been playing Dave the Diver and Overcooked. I especially love Overcooked and its constantly updating maps — it's so much fun! In the future, I'll be exploring more types of games.

AI Invading Daily Life — I recently started using Codex, and I found it can completely replace some of the work I used to do myself, like layout and programming. The results aren't always perfect, but they're pretty close to perfect. It really is amazing how technology is changing life. AI has truly invaded everyone's daily life — my 70-something grandpa now goes to Doubao for whatever question he has, and even the travel itinerary my mom made for our family trip was AI-assisted.

Mixed Feelings About Housework — I have complicated feelings about doing housework, but overall I do like it. Things like laundry and cooking are quite tedious — especially when you have to do them every single day, I often can't be bothered to start. But when I finish everything in one go, I get a strong sense of satisfaction. Maybe it's because usually I have to use my brain in front of the computer for homework, while housework doesn't require much thinking and lets me move my body a little — the two complement each other perfectly.

The Perfect Breakfast / Afternoon Tea — I recently discovered a really delicious breakfast or afternoon tea combo: an iced Americano with a Starbucks chocolate muffin. The bitterness of the iced Americano forms a perfect contrast with the sweetness of the dessert. If you eat the dessert first, when the sweetness starts to get cloying, a sip of the iced Americano not only cuts through the sweetness but also leaves a lingering aroma of coffee in your mouth as a finish. It's amazing!

It was embarrassing at the time, but it became a funny family memory.

The night before an important exam, I stayed awake until nearly three in the morning, reviewing notes and worrying about my performance. My desk was covered with textbooks, empty cups, and handwritten reminders. At some point, I realized that studying more would probably not help. I closed my books and went to sleep. Looking back, that night reminds me of how much pressure I used to put on myself.

During my teenage years, I once had a serious argument with my parents about how I wanted to spend my free time. They believed I should focus more on studying, while I wanted greater independence. The conversation became uncomfortable, and I left the dining room feeling frustrated. However, we discussed the issue again a few days later. It was one of the first times I understood that growing up also meant learning how to communicate different opinions.

One evening, I stood on the balcony with a close friend after we had spent the afternoon together. We talked about our future plans, university, and the possibility of living in different cities. Neither of us knew exactly what would happen next. The conversation was ordinary, but I still remember the atmosphere and the uncertainty we both felt. It was a moment when I began to realize that our lives were gradually changing.

One of my clearest memories is the day I left home to begin university. My suitcase was standing near the entrance, and I kept checking whether I had forgotten anything. My parents reminded me about small practical things, probably because none of us knew what else to say. When I finally closed the door behind me, I felt both excited and strangely emotional. It was the beginning of a more independent stage of my life.

I remember staying up late with my cousin during a family gathering. After everyone else had gone to bed, we sat in the living room and talked about our childhood experiences, school life, and future plans. We rarely had the opportunity to have such a long conversation. Although nothing particularly exciting happened, I remember feeling that we understood each other better afterward.

One afternoon, I realized that I had accidentally deleted a folder containing several weeks of schoolwork from my computer. I spent hours searching for ways to recover the files, but nothing seemed to work. I remember sitting at my desk feeling frustrated and helpless. Eventually, I had to redo most of the assignments. The experience taught me the importance of keeping backups, although it was an extremely stressful lesson.

One year, I had planned a small birthday dinner with my family, but an unexpected disagreement changed the atmosphere completely. What was supposed to be a relaxing evening turned into an uncomfortable conversation, and everyone became unusually quiet. I remember sitting at the dining table, wishing the evening would end sooner. Although the disagreement was eventually resolved, that birthday reminded me that meaningful occasions do not always turn out as expected.

On the evening before my family moved to a new apartment, I spent some time alone in my almost empty bedroom. Most of my belongings had already been packed into boxes, and the room looked unfamiliar without its usual furniture and decorations. I thought about the years I had spent there and the different stages of my life associated with that space. Leaving felt strange because I realized how many ordinary moments had become important memories.

When I was in kindergarten, I was leaning back in my chair during class. I was not paying attention, lost my balance, and fell backward, hitting the back of my head. At first I only felt dizzy. When I reached back and touched it, it felt warm and sticky. I brought my hand in front of me and saw that it was covered in bright red blood. I was taken to the school clinic and then rushed to the hospital, where I got one stitch. For quite a while after that, my head was wrapped in bandages, and I looked like a little “carrot head.”

When I was in kindergarten, we once went on an outing. A woman saw some small green berries by the roadside, picked one, and stuck it into her nostril, pretending it was booger to make everyone laugh. I copied her, but once I put the berry into my nose, I could not get it out. A group of adults gathered around me trying to figure out what to do, but it would not come out and only got pushed farther in. They hurriedly took me to the hospital. On the way there, I was too scared to breathe hard and was so careful that I was almost out of breath. When we arrived, the doctor worked on it for a while and finally removed the berry. I instantly felt relieved, and then my nose started bleeding. It felt like I had narrowly escaped disaster.

When I was in first grade, a teacher gave me a box of Angry Birds shaped erasers. I loved them so much that I played with them during class and after class. But I could not stop thinking about it, and finally I could not resist stealing it back. The teacher was very angry and investigated one by one. I was terrified, and in the end I admitted it. That experience felt so humiliating. Luckily, the teacher understood me and did not scold me too harshly.

When I was in middle school, I was a key player on my class basketball team. My teammates, out of support, didn’t laugh, and our opponents, because they were focused on the competition, didn’t laugh either. But after the game, when everyone talked about it, they all burst into uncontrollable laughter.

As a child, I followed traffic rules very strictly. Everyone laughed, and they all praised me for it.

Before the third grade of primary school, I lived in a remote county town, where I was mostly raised by relatives.

During those years, I often travelled between the mountains and the town to visit my grandparents on both sides of the family. Every time I visited my maternal grandparents, I had to walk for another hour after getting off the bus, passing through fields, forests, and muddy paths.

I still remember that whenever I arrived, my grandfather would have my favourite fish head dish ready for me.

In the first grade of primary school, our teacher gave us a craft assignment.

I decided to make a wooden aeroplane, assembling different pieces of wood like a puzzle. I borrowed a kitchen cleaver from my aunt and slowly carved and shaped the wooden pieces, one by one, before putting them together.

When I brought the aeroplane to school, my teacher was surprised. I was the only child in the class who had completed the project entirely on my own.

It was one of my earliest memories of being recognised for something I had made with my own hands.

In the third grade, I moved to Shenzhen and attended a private school because there was no place available for me in the public school system.

Before that, I had never received any English education. I didn't even know the alphabet.

Because of this, my homeroom teacher took me from classroom to classroom, asking me to stand in front of other students as an example of what not to be.

My academic performance was poor at the time. During a parent-teacher meeting, my mother was deeply upset by my grades.

In the sixth grade, I transferred to a public school.

Science was my favourite subject because we had many opportunities to make things with our hands. On weekends, I often spent hours building architectural models and bridges out of paper, experimenting with their structures.

My science teacher was always encouraging. She was incredibly patient and genuinely appreciated the things I made.

She was my favourite teacher at that age.

During middle school, for reasons I still don't fully understand, many of my teachers were particularly kind to me, even though my academic performance was never especially good.

I often helped them prepare PowerPoint presentations and sometimes even explained parts of their lessons to the class.

But my favourite teacher was my art teacher. She was young, kind, and supportive. I often stayed at school long after classes had ended just to attend her drawing sessions.

During that period, I devoted a great deal of time to drawing, often staying up until midnight to work on my art.

In high school, I was originally in the science stream. Occasionally, I would design and draw posters for school activities.

Because I was relatively good at drawing but only average in science, my art teacher repeatedly encouraged my homeroom teacher and parents to let me switch to the art stream.

In the second semester of my second year, I finally transferred to the school's first and only art class.

What followed was a period of intensive drawing practice, training, and examinations.

After a great deal of effort, uncertainty, and a little unexpected luck, I eventually got into the university I had always wanted to attend.

University was probably the period when my hormones were at their peak. I had a strong desire to fall in love and spent a lot of time trying to meet new people.

Eventually, I started a relationship with one of my classmates.

I remember that she had adopted a stray kitten. It was her kindness that first drew me to her.

We spent four years together, sharing much of our university life.

Later, while I was studying in the UK, she decided to end our relationship.

When I first entered university, I chose to study film.

At the time, I genuinely wanted to become a director. I bought a lot of filming equipment, made travel videos, and organised actors to shoot several short films.

But I never really had anyone to guide me.

One day, I finally gathered the courage to send my work to a professor who taught filmmaking. He recognised the effort I had put in and told me that my work was probably among the top 30% of students in the same field.

Eventually, I decided to give up filmmaking.

I knew how much effort I had already invested, but I began to question whether I had enough natural talent to go much further in that field.

My time in the UK was one of the happiest periods of my life, both personally and academically.

I quickly adapted to the new environment and began exploring ideas and making things freely. My projects brought me a great sense of achievement and made me feel that I was doing something I genuinely loved.

Back then, I had very little to worry about. Apart from my projects, hardly anything else demanded my attention. It was a remarkably pure period of my life, a time when I constantly felt encouraged and inspired.

I also started hiking with my friends. Back then, we barely understood what danger meant. I still remember one trip when we spent an entire day walking through heavy rain, wearing completely inappropriate leather shoes, soaked from head to toe. It was one of the most dangerous experiences I had ever had, but it was also what made me fall in love with nature.

I began to notice things I had never paid attention to before, things that had always been there but somehow remained invisible to me. I slowly learned how to observe the world around me.

Later, a friend and I travelled to many different places together. We carried 20-kilogram backpacks, brought our tents, and camped wherever our journeys took us.

Looking back, those experiences changed the way I saw the world. Nature became more than just a place to visit. It became something I wanted to explore, observe, and understand.

After graduating, I returned to Shenzhen and started working as an interior designer at a company.

At first, I thought it would be exactly the kind of job I wanted.

But gradually, I found myself being asked to copy other people's designs, repeatedly change my proposals to meet demands that conflicted with my values, and work overtime to accommodate those decisions.

Over time, I began to lose my enthusiasm for the interior design industry.

But I knew that I hadn't lost my passion for design itself. What I had lost was my belief in the way design was being practised within that particular professional environment.

So, exactly one year after joining the company, I decided to leave.

One of my earliest memories of drawing is from kindergarten, although some details are blurry now. I drew different vegetables with eyes, noses, mouths, arms, and legs, all holding hands. My teacher praised my drawing. I remember feeling happy that something from my imagination could make someone respond positively. I think this was one of the reasons I began to love drawing.

In primary school, I joined both an art competition training group and a table tennis training group. Their schedules clashed, so my table tennis teacher asked me to leave the team and focus on art. Later, I was also dropped from the art group. I was younger than the other students and felt that I could not learn the drawing techniques as quickly. I felt disappointed because I had given up one opportunity, only to lose the other as well.

After I moved away from home to attend high school, I returned one day and discovered that my childhood drawings were gone. I had kept them on top of a bookcase, but my mother had thrown them away because she thought they were old, dirty, and no longer useful. I was so hurt that I left home for a night. I can understand that she saw those objects differently, but losing them still hurts because they held memories that mattered to me.

In junior high school, I wrote an English script for Cinderella and organized my classmates to perform it. I also played the Fairy Godmother. The rehearsals gave us many happy memories, and I was proud that I could turn an idea into a complete performance with other people. Looking back, I am surprised by how willing I was to take the lead and make things happen.

There was a large green lawn on my university campus, with a huge tree and other beautiful trees around it. During my final year, whenever I felt stressed and could not continue writing, I would ride my electric scooter there and spread out a picnic mat. I would lie down, feel the warm sunlight, and let myself stop thinking about work for a while. As I rested, I felt my body slowly regain its energy.

During university, I worked part-time in a café that also sold bread. The owner and my coworkers were kind, and I enjoyed learning to make coffee, practising latte art, and serving bread to customers. My happiest memory was taking home bread that would otherwise be thrown away after closing and sharing it with my roommates and friends. Learning something new and bringing something back for people I cared about made that period feel especially happy.

On my first solo trip, I travelled from Guangzhou to places including Weihai, Qingdao, and Beijing. Although I travelled alone, I met new people along the way. In Weihai, I met a woman by the sea, and we enjoyed talking so much that we spent the evening eating, walking around, and sharing stories. That experience made life feel like an open-world game: I could set off alone and discover unexpected connections along the way.

Recently, I pursued someone I liked for the first time. Taking the initiative made me feel nervous, excited, and hopeful. However, his responses felt distant, and I gradually felt that my interest was not returned. I felt hurt and discouraged, especially because approaching him had taken so much courage. This memory holds both the excitement of opening up to someone and the disappointment of feeling that they did not want to get closer.

My first real experience of caring for a pet was with a small parrot. I taught it to stand on my hand, peeled sunflower seeds for it, and spent time playing with it. These small interactions made me feel connected to another living creature in a new way. I remember the happiness of being able to interact with it without sharing a human language.

When I first tried pottery, I fell in love with shaping clay with my own hands. I also enjoy flower arranging. In both activities, my hands change the materials, and the materials respond in ways that guide my next move. I become absorbed in adjusting shapes and arrangements, and my attention stays with what is in front of me. Creating things this way feels calming, satisfying, and playful.

It was in September, my grandpa’s funeral.
On the second day, we had a ceremony. We took his spirit to a temple.
Red spider lilies grew all along the road.
All relatives walked there in white mourning clothes.
We had to climb in through a small gate of the temple.
After entering the temple, we walked in the shape of number eight around the Bodhisattva altar.
In the big hall, we burned the chair he used when he was alive.
All family members held hands and made a circle. We turned three times clockwise, then three times counter-clockwise.

What also stays in my mind is this. At first, my family told me that my grandpa was badly ill and I needed to come back quickly. I did not feel very worried at that time. Everyone in the family thought he would not pass away so soon.
I took a taxi home. When I arrived, I saw many wreaths at the gate. Relatives wore white mourning clothes. Any worry any thought was cleard,just felt a shock.
Then my family asked me to see grandpa. He died from cancer. His body became extremely thin. He looked totally different from before. His skin was yellow. I even thought it was a model, not him. He wore a hat I had never seen on him. The temperature was 20 to 30 degrees, but he was covered with thick quilts.
My mum told me to call grandpa and tell him I had come back. But I could not even see things clearly my sight turned blurry and could not say a single word.

I am an art student. I repeated one year of high school. I wanted to get into the best art school. I passed every exam and got the qualification.
In my second college entrance exam, I missed the score for Central Academy of Fine Arts by just 0.5 points. But in Zhejiang Province, art students only had one valid place to choose between key universities and art academies. I failed to get in. I went to a university in Nanjing.

I felt really sad and thought it was unfair. Other students could go to schools matching their scores. But I was transferred to a university far below my score level. I was not willing to accept it. I fell into low spirits for almost two years.

Later I studied hard again and entered HKUST. My teachers told me not to hope for this school at first, because my undergraduate background was not good enough.
During this time, I slowly became independent. I did not depend on my parents to make choices anymore. I fought a lot with myself inside.

At first, I thought being an adult was not different from my teenage life. But after this hard journey, I truly grew up. I am still not fully mature. However, just like a butterfly breaking out of its cocoon, I had a real change in my heart.

My grandmother is already sixty years old now. She always gets up before dawn to work, sometimes as early as four o'clock in the morning. And most of the jobs she takes are very tiring. Occasionally, she just helps out with the activities in the village. The pay is very little, but she remains enthusiastic and never complains. Once I asked her why she could stay energetic when her efforts are not very fairly rewarded. She said, "Doing something is better than doing nothing, and most importantly, these jobs can make her feel useful." She is really content with her life now. The pay is not very important to her. And that makes me really admire her because I always complain about my life. I'm very focused on what I will get or whether these things are fair to me, and I struggle with these things. But now I find that these things exhaust all of my energy. It's not right.
